objectives: State the 6 degrees of freedom + flight axes.

slides.title: Six degrees of freedom + control surfaces
slides.body:
An aircraft has **6 degrees of freedom (6 DOF)**:

**Translations**:
- **X** (forward / aft): controlled by thrust + drag.
- **Y** (lateral): controlled by yaw + bank angle (turn coordination).
- **Z** (vertical): controlled by lift (pitch + speed).

**Rotations** about each axis:
- **Roll** (around X / fuselage): controlled by **ailerons** on wings.
- **Pitch** (around Y / wingspan): controlled by **elevators** on horizontal tail.
- **Yaw** (around Z / vertical): controlled by **rudder** on vertical tail.

**Control surfaces**:
- **Ailerons** (outer trailing edge of wings): differential up/down → roll moment.
- **Elevators** (horizontal tail trailing edge): both up or both down → pitch.
- **Rudder** (vertical tail trailing edge): left or right → yaw.
- **Flaps** (inner trailing edge): increase $C_L$ + $C_D$ for landing + takeoff. Symmetric.
- **Slats** (leading edge devices): high-lift at high angle of attack. Used in landing.
- **Spoilers** (top of wings): destroy lift on landing + drag on descent.

**Multi-axis maneuver**:
- **Coordinated turn**: bank + slight rudder + back-pressure (elevator). Smooth turn.
- **Climb**: pull back on stick (pitch up) + add thrust.
- **Cruise**: trim controls so no force on stick (autopilot-equivalent stable).

**Air-data system**: pitot tubes measure dynamic pressure → airspeed; static ports → altitude; AoA vane → angle of attack. Critical inputs to flight control. Aircraft accidents (Air France 447, AOA-sensor failures on 737 MAX) have been traced to faulty air-data.

**Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU)**: 3-axis gyros + accelerometers. Measure aircraft attitude + acceleration. Required for autopilot + advanced control systems. Modern: MEMS IMUs (~\$10s), aviation-grade fiber-optic (\$10K+), strapdown ring-laser (\$100K+).

slides.title: Static + dynamic stability
slides.body:
**Static stability**: tendency to RETURN to equilibrium after disturbance.
- **Positive (stable)**: airplane corrects itself. Conventional design.
- **Neutral**: stays disturbed.
- **Negative (unstable)**: diverges. Modern fighters intentionally unstable (more maneuverable; computer keeps stable).

**Stability comes from feedback**:
- **Pitch**: tail force balances wing pitching moment + CG. Disturbance → tail responds.
- **Roll**: dihedral (wings angled UP from fuselage) → sideslip increases lift on lower wing → corrective roll.
- **Yaw**: vertical tail provides weathercock stability — flies into the wind direction.

**CG (Center of Gravity)** position critical:
- Forward CG: stable but heavier elevator forces.
- Aft CG: more maneuverable, but if too far aft, NEUTRAL or UNSTABLE.
- Each aircraft has CG limits in pilot's documentation.

**Dynamic stability**: behavior over time after disturbance.
- **Convergent oscillation**: returns to equilibrium with decreasing amplitude. Desirable.
- **Persistent oscillation**: amplitude stays constant. Not great.
- **Divergent oscillation**: amplitude grows. Pilot may not be able to recover.

**Common dynamic modes**:
- **Phugoid**: long-period (30-60 sec) oscillation of pitch + altitude + airspeed. Slow + usually pilot-controllable.
- **Short-period pitch**: faster pitch oscillation (~5 sec).
- **Dutch roll**: coupled yaw + roll oscillation. Common in swept-wing aircraft. Yaw damper (autopilot feature) typically required.
- **Spiral mode**: slow divergent bank tendency. Pilot or autopilot corrects.

**Modern unstable aircraft**:
- **F-16, F-22, F-35, B-2, Eurofighter**: aerodynamically unstable. Computer-controlled (FBW) keeps stable. Without computer, would diverge.
- Allows highly responsive maneuver + reduced trim drag.
- Requires triple-or-quadruple-redundant flight computers.

slides.title: Fly-by-wire + the rise of computer flight control
slides.body:
**Fly-by-wire (FBW)**: pilot inputs go to computers, which calculate control surface positions + drive actuators. NO direct mechanical link.

**Benefits**:
- **Envelope protection**: prevents pilot from exceeding aircraft limits (Gs, AoA, bank angle, airspeed). Reduces accidents.
- **Optimized handling**: same plane can feel like a fighter or transport via gain scheduling.
- **Stability augmentation**: unstable aircraft become flyable.
- **Reduced weight**: no mechanical linkages, no cables.
- **Improved redundancy**: parallel digital channels easier than parallel mechanical.

**History**:
- **Concorde** (1969): some FBW.
- **F-16** (1974): first production fighter with FBW.
- **Airbus A320** (1987): first commercial transport with FBW. Still flying.
- **Boeing 777** (1994): Boeing's first FBW airliner.

**Architecture (typical commercial FBW)**:
- 3-4 redundant flight computers (PRIM, SEC channels on Airbus).
- Different software per channel to avoid common-mode failures.
- Real-time operating system (often verified to DO-178C DAL-A — highest safety level).
- Inertial Reference Systems (IRS) + ADIRU (Air Data Inertial Reference Units) provide state.
- Hydraulic / electric actuators drive control surfaces.
- Backup mechanical reversion in some designs (A320 has direct-link backup).

**Boeing vs Airbus philosophy**:
- **Airbus**: 'hard limits' — flight envelope can't be exceeded (computer overrides pilot).
- **Boeing**: 'soft limits' — pilot can override, but warned. 

Debate ongoing about which approach is safer. Different training implications.

**Notable FBW incidents**:
- **Air France 447 (2009)**: pitot tubes iced; airspeed lost; alpha-prot mode reverted to 'alternate law' (fewer protections); pilots inputs misinterpreted situation; crash. Highlighted importance of pilot training in degraded modes.
- **737 MAX MCAS (2018-19)**: not pure FBW, but partial-automatic stabilizer trim. Single AoA sensor failure caused two crashes. Boeing issue with safety-system design + sensor redundancy.

**Future**: increased automation. Single-pilot operations (SPO) being studied for cargo + later for passenger. Optionally-piloted vehicles + UAVs increasingly common.

question.question: Coordinated turn calculation
question.goal: Aircraft banks at 30° at 150 m/s airspeed. Required pitch + yaw control for coordinated (no side-slip) turn?

steps.prompt: Load factor in banked turn: $n = 1/\cos(\theta)$. At 30°?
Aircraft must increase $C_L$ (pitch up) by ~15% — pull back on stick. Yaw: tail force balances sideforce on fuselage. Coordination via rudder?

options: Small amount of rudder INTO the turn to coordinate (prevent side-slip). The amount depends on adverse yaw from aileron drag. Modern jets have yaw damper + turn coordinator that handle this automatically.

steps.reveal: Small rudder into the turn (left turn = left rudder). Amount calibrated to aircraft. Light singles: pilot inputs rudder. Jets: yaw damper + autopilot coordinate.
~4 km radius. Smaller bank = larger radius. Steeper bank = tighter turn but higher G. Fighters bank 60-90° for tight maneuvers.

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{n = 1/\cos(\theta), r = v^2 / (g \tan \theta)}$$ Basic turn geometry. The trade-off: bank angle vs G-load + altitude loss. 30° bank: 1.15g. 60° bank: 2g. 75° bank: 4g. Commercial aircraft typically limit to 25-30° bank in normal flight; 60° bank max in emergencies. Modern FBW envelope protections enforce limits + smooth pilot inputs.

question.question: Why are modern fighters intentionally aerodynamically UNSTABLE?
options: Statically unstable aircraft are MORE MANEUVERABLE (less restoring moment to fight when changing direction); computer-controlled FBW keeps them stable in steady flight while letting the pilot exploit the maneuverability. Without computer = uncontrollable.
question.explanation: Statically unstable design: no restoring moment, all force-generation goes into maneuvering. F-16 (1974) pioneered. Pros: faster pitch response, less trim drag. Cons: requires continuous computer correction; computer failure = lost aircraft. Multiple redundant flight computers (4× in F-22) keep this safe. Modern designs (B-2 stealth bomber, F-35, Eurofighter) all intentionally unstable.

slides.workedSolution: Unstable aircraft: no restoring force, all forces go into maneuver. Faster + more agile. Requires constant computer correction. F-16 first to demonstrate; modern fighters all FBW + unstable. Reliability requires redundant computers (3-4 channels). Failure modes: redundancy + fallback modes; pure mechanical control impossible. Trade-off: maneuverability for control-complexity. Has paid off.

Airbus A320 'protection' philosophy
question.prompt: The A320's flight control will not allow the pilot to stall the aircraft. Walk through the engineering choices + the trade-offs vs Boeing's more pilot-permissive philosophy.
Explain in two or three sentences why fly-by-wire is now standard on commercial + military aircraft.
question.rubric: Mentions that FBW provides envelope protection (preventing exceeding limits), enables aerodynamic instability (greater maneuverability), reduces weight (no mechanical linkages), eases redundancy + reconfiguration; trade-off is software complexity + dependence on continuous computer operation; modern verified-software techniques (DO-178C) have made FBW reliable enough that it's a net safety improvement.
